name: Bonnor Beam of Light
description: The exact gravitational field of a steady beam of light, which William Bonnor found in 1969, a plane-fronted gravitational wave that keeps pace with the light. A ray moving with the beam feels nothing, a ray moving against it is drawn in, and two beams shining the same way do not attract each other.
convention: We keep factors of $G$ and $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Does light pull on light? Richard Tolman, Paul Ehrenfest, and Boris Podolsky put the question to general relativity in 1931, with Einstein's approximate solution for weak fields, a steady pencil of light, and a passing pulse [tolman1931]. A test ray running parallel to the pencil keeps unit velocity, the same as the light in the pencil itself, and a ray sent in any other direction feels a gravitational action [tolman1931]. A test particle beside the middle of the pencil falls toward it with twice the acceleration a simple application of Newton's theory predicts [tolman1931]. Tolman gave the pencil and the pulse four sections of his textbook of 1934 [tolman1934book].¶John Wheeler took that result into his geons, electromagnetic disturbances held together by the gravitational attraction of their own mass [wheeler1955, faraoni1999]. Two nearly parallel pencils of light, he wrote in 1955, "attract gravitationally with twice the strength one might have thought when their propagation vectors are oppositely directed, and when similarly directed attract not at all" [wheeler1955, faraoni1999]. A class of exact gravitational waves that Asher Peres wrote down in 1959 carries a free profile $f$, and is a vacuum wherever $f$ is harmonic in the two transverse coordinates [peres1959]. Where it is not, he noted, the source of $f$ "can then be interpreted as a null electromagnetic field" [peres1959]. One of those waves, he proposed in 1960, is the field outside a beam of light, and a sum of two the field of a pair of beams [peres1960, bonnor1969light].¶William Bonnor took a doctorate in chemistry in 1946, worked for Shell, and paid for a year of mathematics at University College London with a win on the football pools, by a system he had devised himself [maccallum2015]. By 1969 he was professor of mathematics at Queen Elizabeth College, London, and he went back to Tolman's beams for an exact solution of Einstein's equations [maccallum2015, bonnor1969light]. He took the light to be a fluid of photons all moving one way at the speed of light, and the metrics it sources turned out to be the plane-fronted gravitational waves, "well known already" [bonnor1969light]. A steady beam shining along $z$ adds one term to flat spacetime, $A(x, y)\left(c\,dt - dz\right)^2$, and the Laplacian of $A$ across the beam is proportional to the energy density of the light [bonnor1969light]. The exact solution and Tolman's linear approximation are, he found, "formally identical", since the Ricci tensor of these metrics has no nonlinear terms [bonnor1969light].¶For a uniform beam of circular cross section he joined an interior solution to the vacuum field outside, with the metric and its first derivatives continuous at the edge [bonnor1969light]. Its field is twice that of a rod of matter with the same energy per unit length [bonnor1969light]. Two beams shining the same way add with no extra term in the metric, where two static particles in Weyl's solutions need a strut to hold them apart, so the beams do not interact [bonnor1969light]. In the null coordinates $\sqrt{2}\,u = ct - z$ and $\sqrt{2}\,v = ct + z$, with polar coordinates across the beam, he integrated the geodesics: no particle and no light ray but one parallel to the beam escapes to infinity, and a ray of the beam knocked off line oscillates about its old distance from the axis, so the uniform beam is gravitationally stable [bonnor1969light]. Sunlight falling on the Earth makes a beam of about $6\times10^{-8}$ grams per centimetre, and he judged the new effects too small to detect [bonnor1969light].¶Bonnor also let a pulse sharpen to a delta function, whose field vanishes at every point except at the instant the pulse passes, when it equals that of an infinite rod [bonnor1969light]. From the Schwarzschild metric, by a singular Lorentz transformation, Peter Aichelburg and Roman Sexl arrived at that field in 1971 as the field of a massless point particle [aichelburg1971]. Bonnor gave the fluid a spin in 1970 and found the exterior locally isometric to the exterior of a fluid with none [bonnor1970spin]. Valeri Frolov and Dmitri Fursaev found spinning pulses of radiation again in 2005 and named them gyratons [frolov2005, podolsky2014].¶Slow the light down, as in a waveguide, and two parallel beams do interact [scully1979, schneiter2018]. Marlan Scully calculated in 1979 the field of a laser pulse travelling at less than $c$ and the trajectory of a probe pulse passing through it [scully1979]. For two beams shining in opposite directions the field can stand still: Dietrich Kramer's exact solution of 1998 is static, regular on the axis, and joins smoothly to Levi-Civita's vacuum metric outside [kramer1998]. The missing attraction between parallel beams got its explanation in 1999, when Valerio Faraoni and R. M. Dumse traced it to a gravitoelectric force exactly cancelled by a gravitomagnetic one [faraoni1999]. Light attracts light, they found, four times as strongly as matter attracts matter at equal energy density [faraoni1999]. Two opposed laser beams of one watt, ten centimetres apart, have by their estimate a transverse acceleration per unit length of about $2\times10^{-110}$ per centimetre [faraoni1999].¶Give the pulse a beginning and an end, as Dennis Rätzel, Martin Wilkens, and Ralf Menzel did in 2016, and its gravitational effects are confined to spherical shells expanding at the speed of light from its emission and its absorption, the first drawing a nearby particle toward the track and the second pushing it away [ratzel2016]. A petawatt laser, they estimated, strains spacetime a millimetre from its beam about as much as a gravitational wave of 1 kHz from an astronomical source [ratzel2016]. With diffraction let in, Fabienne Schneiter, Rätzel, and Daniel Braun found in 2018 frame dragging from the beam's spin angular momentum and, at fourth order in the divergence angle, a deflection of parallel beams that overlap it [schneiter2018]. Bonnor was still asking where the field comes from in a paper of 2009: it cannot arise from a retarded potential generated by the photon, he argued, and he suggested it arises as the photon is emitted [bonnor2009]. He died in 2015 at 94, with a paper in refereeing, and Malcolm MacCallum, writing his obituary, counted among his works "the 'Bonnor beam', which models the gravitational field of a beam of light" [maccallum2015].

related.text: The whole family of plane-fronted waves with parallel rays. Bonnor's beam is the member whose profile holds still in time and has light for its source [bonnor1969light].

A pulse of light with no width and no length, the field of one massless particle. Bonnor wrote its profile down in 1969 as the sharpest pulse, and Aichelburg and Sexl reached it in 1971 by boosting Schwarzschild's field [bonnor1969light, aichelburg1971].
The static vacuum outside a line of matter. Two beams shining in opposite directions make a static source, and Dietrich Kramer joined their exact field to Levi-Civita's metric in 1998 [kramer1998].
Another of Bonnor's electromagnetic spacetimes, a bundle of magnetic field lines held together by its own gravity. He found it in 1954, ten years before Melvin [bonnor1954].
The beam switched off. With $A = 0$ the metric is Minkowski's, and on the axis of a uniform beam the plane of $t$ and $z$ is flat with the light still on.
Light as the source again, here streaming out of a point mass and pushing it along. Bonnor named its rectilinear case the photon rocket in 1994 [bonnor1994].
Light as the source again, here streaming out of a star evenly in all directions. Prahalad Vaidya found the field around the star in 1951 [vaidya1951].

coordinates.name: Cartesian

parameters.description: Profile of the beams, a dimensionless function of the two transverse coordinates, with $A \ge 0$. The energy density of the light is $\epsilon = c^4\left(\partial_x^2 A + \partial_y^2 A\right)/16\pi G$, so $A$ is harmonic outside the beams

coordinates.convention: We use William Bonnor's coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and the beams shining toward $+z$, in the signature $(-,+,+,+)$, where his profile $A \ge 0$ enters with a minus sign. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 - A\left(c\,dt - dz\right)^2

coordinates.name: Null Cartesian

parameters.description: Profile of the beams, a dimensionless function of the two transverse coordinates, with $A \ge 0$. The energy density of the light is $\epsilon = c^4\left(\partial_x^2 A + \partial_y^2 A\right)/16\pi G$, so $A$ is harmonic outside the beams

coordinates.convention: We use William Bonnor's null coordinates $\sqrt{2}\,u = ct - z$ and $\sqrt{2}\,v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $x$ and $y$ the transverse lengths and the beams shining along the rays of constant $u$, $x$, and $y$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Null Cylindrical, Inside the Beam

parameters.description: Energy density of the light, uniform across the beam; the energy per unit length of the beam is $\pi R^2\epsilon$

coordinates.convention: We use William Bonnor's null coordinates $\sqrt{2}\,u = ct - z$ and $\sqrt{2}\,v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $\rho$ the distance from the axis of the beam and $\phi$ the angle about it. The light has the uniform energy density $\epsilon$ out to the radius $R$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Null Cylindrical, Outside the Beam

parameters.description: Energy density of the light, uniform across the beam; the energy per unit length of the beam is $\pi R^2\epsilon$

coordinates.convention: We use William Bonnor's null coordinates $\sqrt{2}\,u = ct - z$ and $\sqrt{2}\,v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $\rho$ the distance from the axis of the beam and $\phi$ the angle about it. The beam, of energy density $\epsilon$, fills $\rho \le R$, and the metric and its first derivatives are continuous at its edge. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
